query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Switching the conventional gravity‐casting route to a suction‐assisted (rapid solidification) processing method for HfZrTiTa0.53 will yield a finer, more uniform microstructure that increases tensile ductility and uniform elongation without decreasing the high strength or compromising the impact‐triggered chemical energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 produced by conventional gravity casting, exhibiting a coarse, inhomogeneous grain structure and limited tensile ductility (≈13.5% elongation) with a yield strength around 786 MPa.
generation.intervention: Adopt a suction‐assisted casting (or similarly rapid solidification) process to refine the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Room temperature uniaxial tension tests conducted at quasi‐static strain rates (≈1×10^−3 s^−1) and standardized impact tests (e.g., high‐velocity thin‐steel-target penetration) to verify energy release.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced grain size and a more uniform distribution of grains/boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Rapid solidification minimizes grain coarsening and microstructural heterogeneity, thereby reducing stress concentration sites and delaying premature crack initiation. This process retains the reactive elemental composition (Hf and Zr) that is responsible for the impact‐triggered energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in uniform elongation (e.g., from ~13.5% to >20%) with maintained yield strength (~786 MPa) and unchanged impact-triggered combustion behavior.
generation.baseline: HfZrTiTa0.53 exhibiting 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain, with confirmed impact energy release performance.
generation.boundary: The improvement must not alter the elemental composition critical for energy release and should be effective under room-temperature quasi-static tension and impact test conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative gain in tensile ductility is uncertain and may depend on precise control of the suction-assisted processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 samples—one via conventional gravity casting and one via suction-assisted casting. Conduct identical room-temperature tensile tests at a strain rate of ~1×10^−3 s^−1 and standardized impact tests (e.g., thin-steel penetrator tests) on both sample sets.
measurements: Uniform elongation and tensile ductility from stress–strain curves
Yield strength and other key mechanical properties
Qualitative and quantitative assessment of impact-triggered energy release (e.g., high-speed imaging of impact tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the suction-assisted cast samples do not show a statistically significant increase in uniform elongation (e.g., improvement beyond the baseline of 13.5%) while maintaining comparable yield strength and energy release characteristics, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-energy structural materials (ESMs) integrate a high energy density with rapid energy release, offering promising applications in advanced technologies. In this study, a novel dual-phase Ti40Zr40W10Mo10 high-entropy alloy (HEA) was synthesized and evaluated as a potential ESM. The alloy exhibited a body-centered cubic (BCC) matrix with Mo-W-rich BCC precipitates of varying sizes, which increased proportionally with the W content. The compressive mechanical properties were assessed across a range of strain rates, revealing that the W10 HEA sustained a compressive strength of 2300 MPa at a strain rate of 3000 s−1. This exceptional performance is attributed to the uniform distribution of circular Mo-W-rich BCC precipitates. Conversely, in the W13 HEA, the aggregated and large Mo-W-rich precipitates deteriorated its dynamic properties. Furthermore, deflagration behavior was observed during dynamic deformation of W10, highlighting its potential as a high-performance ESM.Keywords: energetic structural materials, high-entropy alloys, microstructures, mechanical properties
